table.text: The study received approval from the first author's University's ethics committee (ERN_15-1236).
Seven participants were excluded due to attrition, and two were excluded from the initial student cohort for meeting the dyslexia criteria.
Fifty dyslexic adults aged 18-32 years (M=20.7±2.7 years; 27 males) were recruited from universities in the #### #######.

Thirty AWS aged 18-48 years (M=29.5±8.91 years; 22 males) were recruited via targeted outreach within stuttering communities and support organisations such as Stamma, Action for Stammering in Children and universities in the West Midlands.
Prior to the experiment, informed consent was obtained from all participants, and demographic information (age, gender, and handedness) was collected.
Participants were informed that they would complete a naming Stroop task, a suite of individual difference tasks, and two additional tasks not relevant to the current study.

To ensure consistency, all participants completed the assessments in the same fixed order across the sessions (as detailed in Figure 1; see Author et al., 2021 Author et al.,, 2022 Author et al.,, 2023)).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. The experiment had a 2 (congruent: congruent vs. incongruent) x 3 (Group: neurotypical vs. dyslexia vs. stuttering) mixed factor design.
Reaction times (RT; in ms) for correct responses served as the only dependent variable of interest.
The Stroop interference effect was calculated as the RT in the congruent condition subtracted from the RT in the incongruent condition.
Prior to the experiment, informed consent was obtained from all participants, and demographic information (age, gender, and handedness) was collected.
Participants were informed that they would complete a naming Stroop task, a suite of individual difference tasks, and two additional tasks not relevant to the current study.
Throughout the testing session, participants maintained a consistent viewing distance of approximately 60 cm from the display screen.
The study required each participant to attend three separate sessions, with each session lasting approximately one hour.

To ensure consistency, all participants completed the assessments in the same fixed order across the sessions (as detailed in Figure 1; see Author et al., 2021 Author et al., , 2022 Author et al., , 2023)).

text.text: The experimental stimuli for the Stroop task were five colour words ('red', 'blue', 'green', 'yellow' and 'purple') presented in either a red, blue, green, yellow or purple coloured text.
Stimuli were presented against a grey background in white text (Arial, size: 34).
Each participant received five blocks of 20 trials each.
Participants were presented with 75 congruent trials and 25 incongruent trials.

By presenting a higher proportion of congruent trials (e.g., the word "RED" printed in red text), participants develop a stronger expectation for congruence, thus increasing the strength of the Stroop interference effect (see reviews by Algom & Chajut, 2019; Macleod, 1991).

text.text: Within the experiment, the trials were presented in an individually randomised sequence.
Short breaks were inserted after 25 task trials; at this point, participants could continue the experiment by pressing the space key.
Before the experimental trials began, participants familiarised themselves with the task demands in a four-trial practice block.
The stimuli for the practice block were randomly chosen from the set of word-colour combinations.
Each trial started with a white fixation cross that was presented for 500 ms in the centre of the screen.
The fixation cross was replaced by one of the coloured word stimuli, with participants being instructed to name the text colour out loud and to ignore the naming word (Stroop, 1935).

text.text: They did so by speaking into a microphone connected to a Sony DAT recorder (PCM-M1), enabling future offline analysis of the naming data.
This presentation was followed by an inter-trial interval of 1000ms.
This task lasted approximately five minutes.

text.text: Our analytical pipeline comprised two distinct stages: preliminary data reduction and subsequent hypothesis testing.
In the first stage, individual scores were standardized using z-score transformations (scale() in R) to allow direct comparison.

We then calculated Pearson's product-moment correlation coefficients (r) to verify that measures targeting the same theoretical construct were strongly intercorrelated (e.g., nonword repetition and digit memory as indicators of phonological short-term memory; Wagner et al., 1999).

text.text: Once strong intercorrelations confirmed conceptual unity, the corresponding z-scores were averaged into three composite scores.
These three composites were then entered into the PCA alongside five distinct individual difference measures (eight variables total).

Next, only correct trials were included in the RT analyses.

text.text: The current study investigated the question as to whether lexical-semantic processes moderate the suppression of competing responses in Stroop task performance in adult dyslexics, AWS, and neurotypical adults.

We found an elevated Stroop interference effect in both adult dyslexics and AWS compared to neurotypical controls, suggesting lexical-semantic processing impairments during response suppression in both clinical populations.

Because the participant groups were matched on education and non-verbal IQ, these findings provide robust support for a lexical competition impairment in dyslexia, replicating previous work (Kapoula et al., 2010; Stubenrauch et al., 2014; Goranova et al., 2021; Jones et al., 2016) and offer the first standard Stroop evidence for a lexical selection impairment in AWS (Maxfield, 2021).

text.text: The current study also extended previous research by providing a finer grained analysis of performance.
We found that for both dyslexic adults and AWS, Stroop interference was related to varying levels of lexical precision.
Specifically, individuals in these groups with higher levels of lexical precision showed a comparable level of Stroop interference to neurotypical adults.
Conversely, those with lower levels of lexical precision tended to exhibit greater Stroop interference than neurotypical adults.
We found no group differences between dyslexic adults and AWS in the magnitude of Stroop interference that they manifested.

Although we must interpret this finding cautiously due to potential limitations in statistical power and more general caution around interpreting null results, the pattern does align with the LQH (Andrews & Bond, 2009; Andrews & Hersch, 2010; Andrews & Lo, 2013; Perfetti, 2007 Perfetti, , 2019) ) which highlights the crucial role of lexical precision in word recognition.

Furthermore, when comparing the performance of AWS and dyslexic adults, the observed pattern of lexical precision and congruence indicated that higher lexical precision corresponded to less Stroop interference.

In our study, the Stroop interference effect seems to be linked to the underlying quality and accessibility of lexical representations as opposed to purely stimulus-driven lexical competition (see Jones et al., 2010; Maxfield, 2021; Smith-Spark & Moore, 2009).

text.text: Instead, performance variations are better understood as domain-specific nuances tied to automaticity and lexical quality (Perfetti, 2007; Protopapas et al., 2007).

text.text: When an individual's lexical precision is high, word identification reaches a sufficient threshold to trigger standard interference, thus showing preserved competition resolution, as manifested by dyslexic adults and AWS with high lexical precision.

Conversely, large interference effects in individuals with lower lexical precision are suggestive of localized bottlenecks in word-level retrieval as opposed to reflecting a challenge in competition resolution.
Further to these results, we also observed a three-way interaction between lexical precision, group and congruency.

Dyslexic adults with lower levels of lexical precision showed larger Stroop interference than their neurotypical peers, while those with higher levels of the lexical precision component had comparable levels of Stroop interference to the neurotypical adults.
Specifically, higher lexical precision reduces the Stroop interference, allowing dyslexic adults and AWS to achieve sufficient online integration of the Stroop's verbal components.

This outcome is likely due to a subset of dyslexic adults and AWS who through high levels of print exposure and compensatory strategies (Cunningham & Stanovich, 1997; Moll & Bus, 2011; Stanovich, 1986) maintain or achieve higher levels of lexical precision, thereby successfully integrating visual word and colour information to achieve Stroop interference levels comparable to neurotypical adults.

text.text: While robust bottom-up lexical activation is a prerequisite for efficient response suppression in both groups, it would seem that higher lexical precision, regardless of neurodivergent status, equips adults with more efficient conflict resolution abilities.

This efficiency is likely due to more efficient top-down control or compensatory strategies that allow for rapid suppression of competing lexical information, thereby reducing the global interference effect to name the colour (Andrews & Hersch, 2010; Elsherif et al., 2022 Elsherif et al., , 2023;; Perfetti, 2007).

text.text: The current study provides novel insights into the interplay between competition resolution and lexical-semantic processing in dyslexic adults and AWS.
We extend existing hypotheses such as the LQH (Perfetti, 2007 (Perfetti, , 2019) ) by demonstrating that lexical precision moderates Stroop interference in both groups.

text.text: The ability to resolve conflict in the Stroop task is thus not solely a measure of generalised competition resolution but is deeply intertwined with the quality and accessibility of underlying lexical representations.

Our findings align with models that propose that word recognition difficulties in dyslexia stem from not only imprecise phonological representation but also from heightened lexical competition (Goranova et al., 2021; Jones et al., 2016; Nation et al., 2001).

text.text: The pattern of findings observed in the current study is reflective of increased lexical-semantic competition and, for a subset of dyslexic individuals, low lexical precision, which may arise from an over-reliance on lexical and contextual information to compensate for the impairments in grapheme-to-phoneme mappings.
The standard Stroop has not been previously applied to the stuttering population.
The AWS with low lexical precision showed higher Stroop interference than their neurotypical peers, while those with high lexical precision showed comparable Stroop interference.

These novel findings may resolve a broader discrepancy in the literature, where previous naming studies have produced equivocal findings, reporting either no group difference between neurotypical adults and AWS (e.g., Hennessey et al., 2014; Maxfield, 2020 Maxfield, , 2021;; Newman & Ratner, 2007) or longer naming latencies for AWS (e.g., Maxfield et al., 2015).

text.text: We propose that this inconsistency can be explained by variations in lexical precision, which intensify the internal competition during speech planning when a speaker attempts to select a single word from co-activated alternatives that have larger overlap and less differentiation.

This perspective aligns with competitive models of lexical selection, such as WEAVER++ (Levelt et al., 1999; Roelofs, 2018), where a lexical unit is selected only when its activation level surpasses that of its competitors (Roelofs, 2018).

text.text: By incorporating measures that reflect lexical precision (e.g., print exposure, spelling) alongside traditional cognitive impairment (Viesel-Nordmeyer et al., 2023), neurodiversity researchers can move beyond attributing all Stroop performance differences to competition resolution and gain a more comprehensive and nuanced understanding of an individual's cognitive profile and interactions between bottom-up lexical activation and top-down conflict resolution.

text.text: The current study has some limitations that warrant future investigation.

First, within-group analyses did not reveal a significant association between lexical precision and competition resolution in neurotypical adults (n = 84), whereas this relationship was shown in both dyslexic adults (n = 50) and AWS (n = 30) cohorts.
Instead of insufficient statistical power, given that the neurotypical group was our largest cohort, this difference likely reflects a functional ceiling effect in lexical quality.

In neurotypical adults, lexical representation may have reached automatisation, but once lexical precision exceeds this functional ceiling effect, minor individual differences may no longer govern how competition resolution is resolved (e.g., phonological precision; Elsherif et al., 2022), leaving Stroop performance to be perhaps driven by other mechanisms (e.g., domain-general executive control).

text.text: In contrast, the present study showed larger individual differences in AWS and dyslexic adults along the lexical precision continuum, poor lexical representations actively bottleneck competition resolution.

Nevertheless, larger multi-site cohorts, particularly heterogeneous neurodivergent groups such as AWS and dyslexia will be valuable in future work to confirm the stability of these within-group slopes and investigate cognitive subtypes further and in a more finer-grained approach.
In conclusion, the current study provides novel insights into competition resolution within dyslexic adults and AWS by exploring the role of lexical precision in Stroop performance.
We observed that both dyslexic adults and AWS showed a larger Stroop interference effect than neurotypical adults, yet this interference was systematically modulated by lexical precision.
Specifically, individuals with high lexical precision showed Stroop interference comparable to neurotypical readers, while those with lower lexical precision showed greater interference.
Collectively, these findings underscore the intricate relationship between lexical quality, reading experience and competition resolution in these neurodivergent populations.
